title: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring competitors

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring competitors

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring their competitors and enemies; for example, many garden plants that tolerate the local climate never become naturalised because they cannot compete with native plants or resist native animals.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: That climate acts in main part indirectly by favouring other species, we may clearly see in the prodigious number of plants in our gardens which can perfectly well endure our climate, but which never become naturalised, for they cannot compete with our native plants, nor resist destruction by our native animals.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter III, “Struggle for Existence”; section “Effects of climate”. Scope: plants, especially cultivated exotics and native floras

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch03-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Naturalization and climate data permit the abiotic component to be modeled globally, but direct biotic covariates are limited to experiments and local studies. The 'mainly' causal comparison is therefore restricted.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For introduced garden plants that survive cultivation, model naturalization success from abiotic climatic suitability and measured competition or herbivory. Strong biotic effects after high abiotic suitability supports mainly indirect limitation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Competition and herbivory are not globally measured.

Non-naturalization may reflect propagule pressure.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Naturalization inventories, hardiness geography, and traits can test Darwin's garden argument for plants in well-documented regions. That is a restricted and reasonably direct test of indirect limitation. Extending 'mainly' to species in general, and separating competition from propagule pressure, exceeds what those tables cleanly support.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare climate tolerance of cultivated exotic plants with whether they are naturalized, and relate naturalization failure to competitive and enemy-related traits rather than to hardiness. A large set of climate-hardy non-naturalized plants, with naturalization predicted by biotic traits, would support indirect climatic limitation; naturalization predicted by climate tolerance alone would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Garden hardiness and naturalization status are easy to join for some regions and messy for others.

Failure to naturalize can reflect propagule pressure and habitat availability, not only competitors and native animals.

The garden-plant example is narrower than 'climate limits species mainly indirectly' for all species.
